abstract: The form of neural wiring must be robust as well as appropriate for the environment. In resource-rich environments, C. elegans larvae rapidly mature into reproductive adults; otherwise, they enter dauer diapause, a state with altered physiology and behaviors for survival and dispersal from harsh environments. By comparing the electron microscopic reconstruction of multiple dauers and non-dauers, we define two consensus connectomes that stereotypically differ in approximately 1/3 wiring partnerships. We show that these wiring differences result from changes in the availability and selectivity of neurite neighbors to form synapses, as well as how strongly wiring partners choose to connect. We further demonstrate that these changes are best quantified by synapse drive, represented as the density of synapses on available contact, and a pair of synapse drive changes have behavioral consequences. We propose that a connectome results from environment-informed genetic specification of synapse drive, the principal determinant of wiring partnership, among available neurite neighbors.
